subject: history
title: Early Stuarts: James I and the Road to Civil War
welcome_lead: From the Union of the Crowns to Eleven Years' Tyranny.
meta_desc: A-Level Stuart adventure on James I 1603, Gunpowder Plot 1605, Charles I and the origins of the Civil War.
final_note: You can analyse the political and religious tensions of the early Stuart period.

concepts.def: Accession of James VI of Scotland to the English throne on 24 March 1603, joining the two crowns under a single monarch.
Catholic conspiracy by Robert Catesby and others, including Guy Fawkes, to blow up Parliament on 5 November 1605; foiled the night before.
Doctrine, articulated by James I (e.g., The True Law of Free Monarchies), that monarchs derive authority from God alone.
Parliamentary statute extracted from Charles I forbidding non-parliamentary taxation, arbitrary imprisonment and billeting.
Charles I's 'Eleven Years' Tyranny' governing without Parliament; raised funds through Ship Money and prerogative levies.
Two Anglo-Scottish wars triggered by Charles's attempt to impose a new prayer book on Scotland (1637); forced recall of Parliament.

walkthroughs.body_html: James VI/I sought a closer Anglo-Scottish union (rebuffed 1604-07). The Hampton Court Conference (1604) disappointed Puritans but produced the Authorised Version (1611). The Gunpowder Plot intensified anti-Catholic legislation. Tensions with Parliament rose over impositions, the Great Contract (1610) and Spanish Match diplomacy. The Thirty Years' War (from 1618) drew in his daughter Elizabeth.

Charles inherited Buckingham as chief minister, an unpopular figure assassinated in 1628. War with Spain (1625-30) and France (1627-29) drained funds. Forced loans and arbitrary imprisonment (Five Knights' Case, 1627) provoked the Petition of Right (1628). The Three Resolutions (March 1629) accusing ministers of Arminianism preceded eleven years without Parliament.

Wentworth's 'Thorough' governed Ireland; Laud's reforms enforced ceremonial Anglicanism. Ship Money extended from coastal counties to the whole kingdom (Hampden's Case, 1637). The 1637 Scottish Prayer Book triggered the National Covenant (1638) and Bishops' Wars. Defeat forced the calling of the Short Parliament (April 1640) and Long Parliament (November 1640).

mcqs.q: Which 1605 plot aimed to blow up Parliament?
options: Gunpowder Plot
Babington Plot
Ridolfi Plot
Throckmorton Plot

mcqs.q: What was the 1628 statute curbing Charles I's prerogative known as?
options: Petition of Right
Habeas Corpus Act
Triennial Act
Bill of Rights

mcqs.q: Was the English Civil War caused by religion alone?
options: It was caused by Henry VIII's break with Rome.
The Civil War began because Cromwell wanted to be king.
No — religion (Laudian reforms, Scottish Presbyterians) combined with financial disputes (ship money), political conflict over parliamentary rights, and Charles I's personal style.
The Civil War was a war of religion between Catholics and Protestants.

mcqs.q: What caused the English Civil War?
options: Long-term tensions over royal absolutism, religion (Laudian reforms), and parliamentary rights, combined with Charles I's specific mismanagement and personal rigidity.
It was caused by Charles I trying to arrest five MPs in 1642.
It was caused by Henry VIII's break with Rome.
The Civil War began because Cromwell wanted to be king.

mcqs.q: Why is 1688 called the Glorious Revolution?
options: Parliament invited William of Orange to replace the Catholic James II, with little bloodshed in England, establishing parliamentary supremacy and the 1689 Bill of Rights.
William of Orange was Charles II's son and inherited the throne.
It was caused by Henry VIII's break with Rome.
It was glorious because no one died anywhere in the conflict.
